Council meet- ing of this society was held in the nmnts of the society of Arts, in Adam-street, Adel*, London, on Tuesday. Colonel Brim, AI.P., in the chair.—The secretary having read the minutes of the last meetiug, the treasurer, Mr. Clay, reported that the financial condition of thia rociety was in a prospe oils chute..—A report from the committee appointed to consider the propos,' appointinent of a Minister of Agricultare was rtetived, and it was agreed to accept the invitations of the Chambers of Commerce, to meet their deputatiens, and pro- ceed threct to the Prime Minister Vial at petition in favour of such appointment. —lord Carington, WllO VGio received with some cheers, moved the following resolution, of which he had given notice :—.That this Council desires to express a general approvel of the measures introduced hy the late Government.and trusts that the present Adminietration will give early attention to the question of the reformer the Land lows." He argued against the law of enhail, which crippirel the landlord. and put it entirely mit of his power to give relief to the tenant..fariner in time of dietress or to obtain capital for him to properly till the soil. There were ob- stinate mermen. to it in the form of etatesmen who were territorial magnaten, as the Duke of Rielimiond and the Moe (pie of Salisbury ; and secondly, there were the landed gentry, who had purses well lined, such as Mr. Chaplin, who expreesed very Wrong opinions againet the views he entertained—to enable the tenants for life to burden the estate with loans, or null portions of the land If tiny could thereby permanently im- prove the property. It was mid that they meld aff.wd to guarantee 5 percent., on which 'mine advances would be made to tenants ; but there were seasone when landlords haul to allow 20 per ceut. and eveu 50 per cent. to tenants who were unable to pay their rent. Then there was the legal obstruction which could ouly be eet aside by Padie- mentary decision. The pant Lieverninent had done much to . intraluce a bill of relief, and he hoped that ho-newt Govern-I ment would follow up the example set them on this subject. —Mr. Snell considered that the present Government would he more likely to assist in facilitating the transfer of land • than their predecessors .ind as this wan imputent he most cordially seconded Lord Carington's .notion.—The Marquis of thirdly, though differing front the late Government politically, thanked them for some measures, and mere especially for the Contagious Diseases Bill. Ile cordially endorsed the movement. in favour of early transfer of land. If that were not done, when property came into the market three would soon be no purchawra.—After a good deal el discuseion, the motion, with slight alteration, was put and carried unenimously.—Mr. Hodges (Kant Kent) moved— " That, in the opinion of this Council, the present unequal chargee for the nuriage of English and foreign produce act unfairly on the home produce, and inn legitimate euhject for rurther, inquiry."—The Marquis of Huntly two-ended the motion, which was carded lmeniutoualy.—Sir Baldwin Leighton, Air, thought the matter a Very important one, but hop,' it might be' referred to a seleet agrlewitural maw. mittee. " 'BLANC Tnrrn" in Pu;s.—l r'erently gained a little ex- with regard to pigs that may prove modal to some , of your readers,. I know it will to myself. The other day we had a very nice farrow of twelve pigs out of a well-bred white now by spore Berkshire boar. Two were found dead at the end of twenty.four hours and two more the following day, and none of them showed signs of having Well laid , upon. I happened to be there when the last one was brought out of the sty, and on looking it over my attention was called to the frayed condition of its tongue. •'lll be , bound to say it has • black teeth,'" was the innmdiate re- mark of the bailiff, who was standing by, and on examin- ing it his surmise was found to be correct. There they were, one on either side of the top jaw, long and blaek, \Mt as sharp as a needle. After this we watched the sow, and nobd that . soon as the little on. attempted to suck she got up, and moral angrily away. The huh, things had evidently been starved. We then examined tho whole litter and found them All alike. The evil was soon remedied with a pair of pincers, with which the teeth were lar..ken out, and now I am glad to say the remaining eight are doing as well IAR pigs can do. The bailiff nays lie has hid several similar cases in his time ; and he .serts that, as long as we use the same hoar, the same result will follow. This, however, re- mains to be proved. I suliaequently mentimied the matter to two neighbouring farmers, both clever, practical men, and both pig-breeders, and they both assured me they had never beard of such a thing as black teeth." Like myself, how- ' ever, they could both see in it a very probable explanation of various I.ses hitherto inexplicable. On MOTION:An INGENIOUS COPISPIZACT.— The business of like [louse of Commons for each es ening is set forth in an agenda called "The Orders of the Gay," The first procedure, after the Speaker's cry of " Order ! order !" follows umm the stroke of half-past four and in- noulleeki the commencement of public hostile., is the giving of notices of nmtion. It it, of course, desirable th-t a favouraMe oc.sion should be se..l by a member having charge of • motion, and there bI emsequently much manoeuvring for precedence. The stratig, in the gallery will hear tire Speaker c ill out the names 4.f members in what appears to Le chance succession. The mend.: ad- drowsed will thereupon noise, read out his notice, and give place to another in quite a differed part of the House, upon whom the eye of the Sp.ker may, still by chance. it appears, next have fallen. But no place is left for ch.. in Itatglish Parliamentary procedure. What really happens In respect of the notices of motion is this: —On the table at 1601 the clerks nit there lies a long sheet of t.per, ruled, and having printed figures down the side of it. Mei:she's desiriog to gave notice of utotion go up to the table, and write their names. this hi.t. Small bits of paper, bearing numbers corrmponding to those on the list, are twisted of, and plit.d in a box before the clerk. When noticoo of motion " are .11eil on, the clerk puts his in the box, and drawn out one of the Mee. of paper, calling aloud the number he finds thereon—say the figure is 44, and that, to use a name not unfamiliar on the notice paper, Air. Pak nen has chanced to write his name on the line numbered 44. The clerk calls out the number ; the Speaker, who has meanwhile been furnimed with the list of klaklllefl, on ring to to it, duds that Mr. Parnell is nuntl.r 44, alkd those- .. calls Inin by name. Mr. Parnell thus has the first ; choice of unoccupied days within the peri.l of one month ; from the dote of the tithing. The Kneen IS repeated till the contents of the box are exhausted, and the list of notices is concludost Ikletio,l are taken in the House in the onler in which notice has been given, and it is obviously a matter of ',rime importance to obtain a good position. . . In the weeion of Irld an ingenious conspiracy was entered upon by the Home Rule members, with the object of oh- taMing what the Speaker subsequently stigmatised as '• an unfair advantage" in r.pect of precedence for notices of I motion. They had agreed upon a group of notate ten nub- 'eon, which they desired to bring under the notice of the Douse. There being at the time .b ,an forty Flame Rulers In attendance at the /louse, copieo of them ten motions were placed in the hands of meh, with a COMMINI understanding as to which it was most desirable tu give preference. The I whole forty then verote their names down on the notice paper, and, of course, each had a chance in the ballot box. Go the names being called out, the first lion. Ruler who got a phee gave notice to move for I.ve to introduce the particular measure, or to move the particular resolution, which it had been privately agreed was of prime import- ance. The second man called secured the next belt place open for the measure of second importance, and 00 on, through the list. The chance, of any particular measure which the Home Rulers had in charge were thus exactly forty to .e against the opportunity of any measure which any other private member advocated. The plan mceeederl admirably, and the Elonse was mystified and aurprh.ed at the good luck which attended Home Rule members, and secured for them the b.t nights of the sewion. Some weeks later, when all the mischief was done,Captain Ritchie drew the attention of the Sp.ker to the facts. Ihrtstons.—Woo ('yv THE Ble, Wlttn.--On party di- visions, the tellers are the Whips on either side. In division, on questions raised by private members and opposed by the Government, the mover and seconder tell for " the motion," and the Ministerial Whipe for " the Government." A di- vision being insisted on, the Speaker directs strangers to withdraw, and simultaneously a Rtitlel-g1338, which stands on the clerks' table, in turned, and through all the passagee and committee rooms of the House is heard the tinkling of the electric bell. Formerly the order for strangers to withdraw wan literally carried out, the strangers' galleries being cleared. But now only the seaon under the gallery, to which a few strangers are tabnitted by special order, are cleared—a re.monable precaution, seeing that theoo seats are actually on the floor of the House, and (as has happened, at least once, according to well-authenticated history) a stranger straying into the lobbies might actually figure . a unit M the division list. The .nd.glass talus two minute, to run one. during which time the belle are furiously twanging all over the House and hon, mentbers, who have been in the reading-room, library, dining-room, or even oat on the terrace, come hurrying in to vote. When St. Stephen's Club was opened, its pros irbity to the House suggested tho convenience of connecting it with the system of divieion bells, no that supporter. of tbe Government, accustomed to congrezate there, might have due notice of a pending division. One night, during the session of 1175,. Bill, in which the Hanle Rule members were d.ply inter- ested, was in Committee. The supporters of the Government were so far amenable to the injunctions of the Whip that they would come in to vote ; hut they positively declined to remain to hear the debate. Thus, whenever a clause woe reached on which a division was challenged, there waa the sound of hurrying feet along the subway that connects the Club with the House, and an overwhelming contingent of hon. members arrived in time to vote down the opp.ition. About eleven o'clock a most important clause was reached, and a division Iv. challenged. The electric bolls rang out the usual summons ; hut,to the consternation or Sir William Dyke and Mr. Winn, and to the unutterable indignation of Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, then Secretary for Ireland, the Ministerial majority mysteriously diminb.hod, and even vanished, the Home Rulers carrying their point. Upon investigation, it wasdiscovered that soinetlainghad happened to the common ration between the division bell of the House and the 1.1 in St. Stephen's Club—it woo in the days of the late Mr. Ronayne, who Ir. a practical engineer as well a. a man of gr.t humour—and the indignation of the Minis- terial Whip was equalled only by the consternation of the contingent of hon. members at the Club when they heard there had been a division.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SAYLIWAY, MAY 8, PAW.

Two Raw, Canon Ent; the Proteatant Bishop- delineate of Liverpool, has discovered that that dread personage, the Devil, it not dead ! The dinoovery was made by the worthy Divine when advoc.ting the muse of the Church Miaattmary Society in London the other evening, and the diecovery led to another revela- tion—that "there in even now • rock ahead in the appointment of a ROlnklll Cetholie as the new Voseroy of Diehl." Wont the Deed has had to do with putting I 'the rock ahead ''—the appointment of the Marquis of Ripon . the new Viceroy of India—the reverend Canon doea not make quite dear. But it is patent I that either the Devil, Mr. Gladstone, or the Sovereign is at fault, for one of the trio has amusedly had . a hand in the selection of the Catholic Mnrq de as the Vice.regal Governor of India. If hi. Satanic Majesty now appoint. Indian Vieeroys, the title of Empreas of India in a veritable "Benjamin', mete," and the Empress is no E opress, whilst Mr. Gladstone, the professed and ackuneledged guardian and executant of the Conntitution, in under an hallucination in think- ing he has bad a hand in choosing the Marquis aa Lord Ly eon's succession There may boo trinity in the Devilhead that has not yet dawned upon minds other than that of the Protestant Bishop elect of Liver- , pool, and perhaps her rafter we shall be favoured with an elucidation of a mystical trinity io uslity. If the Devil has been wronged in having this heinous , charge laid to his aostunt—well, we suppose, he can hear it. The lellen Angel, we should think, has beenrne hoary with oboe° ; for many thousande of yearn , he ha. borne the beating of the drum ecclesiastic, and if it were some tiny discovered that he is actually dead it would be either a joyous or • Barry day for the , drummers. If either the Sovereign or the Prime , Minister have been wrongly aumpected of having tr.. (erred their _wivilegea and prerogatives to the Evil • One, they won't ho much ruffled by it. They have the aneuranoe of !Sir Richard Aesheton Cross, C.C. 8., , that "there is a lying spirit abroad," and in this they will find comfort and solace. In the utterance, of the Bishop•desiguate there is an evidence of the " activity of the It spirit of religious prejudice and intolerance, and we regret to find that some of our , Scotch Presbyterian friend., evince oven more religious bitterness than Canon Ryle does. The Inver.. Free: , Presbytery is to moved at the appointment of the Marquis of Ripon to the Alt. of Viceroy of Indin! that it has resolved to tend to the members of the '1 Cabinet a communication to the effect " that the , Preebytery strongly dittapprovea of the appointment of • the Mexquie of Ripon, • Roman Catholic, and a recent pervert from Proteetantism, to the office a Viceroy of • ; India." One spenker wan so shocked that he said the appointment was a dreadful one, and a Mi. Mackay ' was no put about that he confesned he was irritated that a pervert should ho sent to India. When will these Christians show to the world that Chnetianity has at leant taught them to accept the Mesaiah'e com- mand, "Love ye one another," instead of nursing petty spiteful jealousies against each other in affairs of State? Whether there who like to hang their religion on the IMI of the State, or believe it incumbent upon them to signal out for contempt and ridieule, on religion. grounde, , acts which concern simply and solely the temporal government of the State, know it or not now, they will have to realiee the fact ere beg that the promulgation of creeda and dogmne is one thing end the Govern- ment of the State is another. Religious supremacy and bigotry have been long on their trial, and the bar- rier. of intoleranew must by the multiplications and growth of einem. and 1/111111 of all sorts and kinds ;in the land, be swept any. In the recent political movementa, too, religions nupremaey and intolerance I have been slaeken to their foundations, and the wholt, euperetructure miS, corner or later, tumble into ruins, and the earlier it does 00 the better it will be for the State and religion ineelf. As Lord Macaulay remarked, in one of his most brilliant pasaagee, "Those who , threet temporal sovereignty or temporal power upon • the Church of Christ treat her . their prototypes treated her illustrious Author. They bow the knee, but they spit upon her ; they cry !' but they smite her on the cheek; they put a sceptre in • her hand, but it is a fragile reed, they crown her, but it is with thorns ; they cover with purple the oronnde their own hands have inflicted, and inscribe magniffent title. over the crow on which they have fixed her to perinh in igno- miny and pain." The march of freedom and ' equality hea been too steady and etrong to allow of a resurrection at this day of that apirit of Protestant asemadaney that once decreed that a man was unfit to enter the portals of Par. liament, to be a Town Councillor, or to be even a Corporate etreet sweeper, unless he was reedy to take oath that he accepted the Protestant faith and partook of the sacrament administered

according to the ceremony of a dominant church by hands rendered holy by episcopal ordinance. It must not be forgotten by thoee who would revive religious exclusiveness that the penal , laws have been abrogated which kept Roman Catholic. from Parliament, from the magistracy, from the Corporations, from the bench, and from the bar; that ' denied them the right to vote at Parliaments/7 elec• tiuns; that disqualified them from acting m °oust:shim, or al.enfis, or jurymen, or in the army or navy , that excluded them from the Universities, forbade them to marry Protestants, consigned them to ignorance un- lees willing to be educated no Protest:ante : that denied them the right to buy land ; that disinherited them of property, and gave it to Protestant informers and that permitted other illiyaltirs in the name of religion to keep in tke necesninin one of the sect+, of the

Christi. Church. One after another res,atjen blows have been struck at petty l alms religious domino- Lion, and ultimately it will he killed outright and in. tarred a itbout hcpe of • resureeetion. Catholic Emm- i cipstion made the hateful thing totter ; the repeal of , the Teets and Corporations Acts wound. dit seriously the removal of taxes on knowledge and the abolition of religious tents in Uni versitire made it stagger t the • diseetablishmelat of the Irish Church and the creation of a national system of slementary eduoation made it reel and now with the return of Mr. Bradlaugh for , Northampton and the appoiwinent of the Marquis of I Ripon as the vioetretral repnwentatire of the Queen en Indite, it is ready to fnfl. The puzzle is known as the "fifteen puzzle." ft consists of fifteen square lick,, numbering fnint one to fifteen, placed it, any position M a equate capable of holding sixteen lilocks. div.p: RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.

The first session of thie enocethful eociety was brought to a dice by a so;rer on Tuesday evening, in Bethesda School- room. A very large number of members and their friends eat down to to excellent tea, provided by Mr. J. Knowles, after which an entertainment was given by several Wiesen,/ gentlemen, under the presidency of the Speaker, Mr. T. Handley. Al the doer. the Premier, Mr. W. J. Shore, amide loud cheers, proposed a cordial vote of thanks to the Speaker for presiding that evening. and for his services as Speaker of the Runcorn House of Commons The motion was seconded by the Member for Leominster, Mr. W. Lyon, in the absence, through indispoeition, of the Leader of the Opimsition. Mr. J. Craig. In referring to the conduct of the Speaker at the sittings of the House. Mr. Lyon said he had not seen a single movement on his part which would lead anyone to suppoee that he leaned to one eide of ths House or the other: and a gentleman en well acquainted with the rules of Parliamentary delate, and th unbiassed in earrvieg them out, deserted their warmest thanks. The Speaker briefly responded, and the room was cleared for dancing, and several couples availed themselves of the opportunity. It may be interesting to notice that the Ministry which hoc been in aMee during the sethion. cod which still retain office during the iminmer recess, is Conertvative, and is composed of nrst Lord of the Treamry, Mr. W. .1. Shore; Foreign Seem- tarry. Mr. J Meadowcroft ; Home Secretary, Mr. C. Gerrard ; Chioacello, of the Exchequer, Mr. 11. Rhoden: Attorney- Geom.'. Mn. F. A. Lake: Indian Secretarv.Mr.J R.Digges. Colonial Secretary, Mr. F. Lightborn ; War Secretary, Mr. A. C. Clandef. . Whip, Mr. 1.. Croeby and Mr. W. Rhodes. A second reconnsiamee took place on Saturday last with the A, B. and C troops of this fine regiment of Yeomanry Cavalry. Amongst the officers present were Major Gerard, C.lptain the Hon. W. C. (ierard, Captain B. Relf (Adjutant), Lieutenant Arthur Gladstone, Lieutenant Humphrey Walmeley, Surgeon Beaman, kc.

Being that an enem;r7e-f;;;;;-;t:p-p—osed to be advancing north.west, ridll Leigh, Bickerehaw, anti Pla't Bri lge, on Neretnn-le-Willows, the troops at Ashton and More Rank were ordered to make • reconnairtance in the above-named direction. and ascertain the exact route taken by the main body of the enemy. The C troop, under the command of its officers, repr,ented the enemy. and proceedvd to Luke's (litter+, Lowton, with instructions to advance on Newton-le-Willows at 330 pm., their Lsnindary being on the right Ooltgene-lane and Rob-I.e, and on their left. l'ark.road to Wargrave. This force represented a squadron, and was ordered to conceal as fora ponsible the advance of the main body by keeping well under cover, sending forward patrds and making feint atMcke on the position at point!, imitable, and drive in the patrols of the defending !force if inferior in numbers, and to advance cautiously with the main body to the !Nestles at Newton.le4Ml illows.

tinder the command of it officers wee ordered to send patrols on all the roads to the front, in the direction named in the "General Idiot," keeping within the boundary the patrols to keep up constant communication, and to .end in written reports of the enemy's movements to Major Gerard. at the head rpm-tore in the Menne,.

About four o'clock the scout of the defending force re- ported that the enemy hid been seen advancing on Newtoo• le-Willows, via Onlbome Smithies and Rob -lame ; almost ' simultaneously a retmrt was brought in by the patrols on the Winwick-toad to the effect that the main hotly was advancing in that direction it. however, turned not Chit the p ttrols were deceived, as the mein body of the enemy at 430 pee.. very cleverly succeeded in getting through the position on the Menu., via Southworth- road, posing under the railway arches, and skirting the Old , Mill and Newton Hall, thereby effectively cutting off a portion of the defending force. The officers and men took a warm interest in the work, and carried not the orders of CaMain H. Melt with cheerfulness and epirit. The mid sketches and reporte eent in by both officers and men were very commendable, and will be.preeented Co the forthcoming inspection at Southport. The day wee all that could be desired for the display, which in all reepects was carried out ye manner gratifying to the officer. and most compli- mentary In the mendere.
